paragraphs: It was a warm, bright day at the end of August. The meeting with the elder had been set for half-past eleven, right after late mass. Our visitors did not attend the service. They arrived just as it ended. First came an elegant open carriage drawn by two valuable horses, carrying Miüsov and a distant relative of his, a young man of twenty named Pyotr Fomitch Kalganov. The young man was getting ready to enter university. Miüsov, with whom he was staying for the time being, was trying to persuade him to go abroad, to the university of Zurich or Jena. The young man had not yet made up his mind. He was thoughtful and absent-minded. He was good-looking, strongly built, and fairly tall. At times his gaze had a strange fixity. Like all very absent-minded people, he would sometimes stare at a person without seeing him. He was silent and rather awkward. But sometimes, when he was alone with someone, he became talkative and gushing, and would laugh at anything or nothing. His liveliness vanished as quickly as it came. He was always well dressed, even elaborately so. He already had some independent money and expected much more. He was a friend of Alyosha’s.

A long way behind Miüsov’s carriage came Fyodor Pavlovitch with his son Ivan, in an ancient, jolting but roomy hired carriage drawn by a pair of old pinkish-gray horses. Dmitri was late, though he had been told the time the evening before. The visitors left their carriage at the hotel outside the monastery grounds and walked to the monastery gates. Apart from Fyodor Pavlovitch, none of them had ever seen the monastery, and Miüsov had probably not set foot in a church for thirty years. He looked around with curiosity and an air of assumed ease. But apart from the church and the service buildings, which were ordinary enough too, he found nothing of interest inside the monastery. The last of the worshippers were coming out of the church, bareheaded and crossing themselves. Among the humbler people there were a few of higher rank, two or three ladies and a very old general. They were all staying at the hotel. Beggars at once surrounded our visitors, but none of them gave anything, except young Kalganov. He took a ten-copeck piece out of his purse and, nervous and embarrassed (God knows why!), hurriedly gave it to an old woman, saying, “Divide it equally.” None of his companions said a word about it, so he had no reason to be embarrassed. But when he saw that, he felt even more flustered.

It was strange that nobody seemed to expect them, and that they were not received with any special honor. One of them had recently donated a thousand roubles, and another was a very wealthy and highly educated landowner on whom everyone in the monastery was in a sense dependent, since a ruling in the lawsuit might at any moment put their fishing rights in his hands. Yet no official came out to meet them.

Miüsov looked absent-mindedly at the tombstones around the church. He was about to say that the dead buried here must have paid a pretty penny for the right to lie in this “holy place,” but he held back. His liberal irony was quickly turning almost into anger.
“Who the devil is there to ask in this idiotic place? We must find out, because time is passing,” he said suddenly, as if talking to himself.

All at once an elderly, bald man came up, with ingratiating little eyes, wearing a full summer overcoat. Lifting his hat, he introduced himself in a honeyed lisp as Maximov, a landowner from Tula. He at once took up our visitors’ problem.
“Father Zossima lives in the hermitage, apart from the rest, four hundred paces from the monastery, on the other side of the copse.”
“I know it’s on the other side of the copse,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, “but we don’t remember the way. It’s a long time since we were last here.”
“This way, through this gate, and straight across the copse ... the copse. Come with me, won’t you? I’ll show you. I have to go.... I’m going there myself. This way, this way.”

They went out of the gate and turned toward the copse. Maximov, a man of sixty, ran rather than walked, turning sideways to stare at them all with an unbelievable degree of nervous curiosity. His eyes looked ready to pop out of his head.

“You see, we’re going to the elder on business of our own,” said Miüsov sternly. “That person has granted us an audience, so to speak. So although we thank you for showing us the way, we can’t ask you to come with us.”
“I’ve been there. I’ve been there already; _un chevalier parfait_,” and Maximov snapped his fingers in the air.
“Who is a _chevalier_?” asked Miüsov.
“The elder, the splendid elder, the elder! The honor and glory of the monastery, Zossima. What an elder!”
But a very pale, worn-looking monk of medium height, wearing a monk’s cap, overtook them and cut short his rambling talk. Fyodor Pavlovitch and Miüsov stopped.
The monk gave an extremely courteous, deep bow and announced:
“The Father Superior invites all of you gentlemen to dine with him after your visit to the hermitage. At one o’clock, no later. And you too,” he added, addressing Maximov.

“I’ll certainly come, without fail,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, enormously pleased at the invitation. “And believe me, we’ve all given our word to behave properly here.... And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, will you go too?”
“Yes, of course. What did I come for, if not to study all the customs here? The only thing in my way is your company....”
“Yes, Dmitri Fyodorovitch doesn’t exist yet.”
“It would be a fine thing if he didn’t turn up. Do you think I like all this, and in your company too? So we’ll come to dinner. Thank the Father Superior,” he said to the monk.
“No, it’s my duty now to take you to the elder,” answered the monk.
“In that case I’ll go straight to the Father Superior—to the Father Superior,” babbled Maximov.
“The Father Superior is busy just now. But as you like—” the monk hesitated.
“Impertinent old man!” Miüsov said aloud, as Maximov ran back to the monastery.
“He’s like von Sohn,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said suddenly.
“Is that all you can think of?... In what way is he like von Sohn? Have you ever seen von Sohn?”
“I’ve seen his portrait. It’s not the features, it’s something you can’t quite name. He’s a second von Sohn. I can always tell from the face.”

“Ah, I’m sure you’re an expert in that. But look here, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you just said that we had given our word to behave properly. Remember it. I advise you to control yourself. But if you start playing the fool, I don’t intend to be associated with you here.... You see what a man he is”—he turned to the monk—“I’m afraid to go among decent people with him.” A fine smile, not without a certain slyness, appeared on the pale, bloodless lips of the monk. He made no reply, and was clearly staying silent out of a sense of his own dignity. Miüsov frowned more than ever.
“Oh, devil take them all! A show put on for the outside, built up over centuries, and nothing but charlatanism and nonsense underneath,” flashed through Miüsov’s mind.
“Here’s the hermitage. We’ve arrived,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “The gates are shut.”
And he crossed himself again and again before the saints painted above the gates and on either side of them.

“When you go to Rome, you must do as the Romans do. Here in this hermitage there are twenty-five saints being saved. They look at one another, and eat cabbages. And not one woman comes in through this gate. That’s what’s remarkable. And that really is so. But I did hear that the elder receives ladies,” he suddenly said to the monk.

“Women of the people are here too just now, lying in the portico there, waiting. But for ladies of higher rank, two rooms have been built next to the portico, but outside the grounds—you can see the windows—and the elder goes out to them by an inner passage when he is well enough. They are always outside the grounds. There is a lady from Harkov, Madame Hohlakov, waiting there now with her sick daughter. He has probably promised to come out to her, though lately he has been so weak that he has hardly shown himself even to the people.”

“So there are loopholes after all, to slip out of the hermitage to the ladies. Don’t think, holy father, that I mean any harm. But do you know, on Athos not only are visits from women forbidden, but no creature of the female sex is allowed—no hens, no turkey-hens, no cows.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, I warn you, I’ll go back and leave you here. They’ll throw you out as soon as I’m gone.”
“But I’m not getting in your way, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. Look,” he cried suddenly, stepping inside the grounds, “what a valley of roses they live in!”

Though there were no roses now, there were masses of rare and beautiful autumn flowers growing wherever there was room for them, plainly tended by a skillful hand. There were flower-beds around the church and between the tombs. The one-story wooden house where the elder lived was also surrounded by flowers.

“And was it like this in the time of the last elder, Varsonofy? He didn’t care for such elegance. They say he used to jump up and beat even ladies with a stick,” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, as he went up the steps.

“The elder Varsonofy did sometimes seem rather strange, but a great deal of what’s told about him is foolishness. He never beat anyone,” answered the monk. “Now, gentlemen, if you’ll wait a minute, I’ll announce you.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, for the last time, remember your promise, do you hear? Behave properly or I’ll make you pay for it!” Miüsov had time to mutter once more.

“I can’t think why you’re so worked up,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said sarcastically. “Are you uneasy about your sins? They say he can tell from a person’s eyes what he’s come about. And how much you think of their opinion, you, a Parisian, and so advanced! I’m surprised at you.”
But Miüsov had no time to answer this sarcasm. They were asked to come in. He walked in, somewhat irritated.
“Now, I know myself. I’m annoyed, I’ll lose my temper and start quarreling—and lower myself and my ideas,” he thought.
